=== DEFECTS FOUND (both reproduced; neither blocks, both should be fixed before this rule is armed to deny) ===

FINDING A -- AN ALLOWLISTED CATEGORY IN A COMMAND CHAIN SUPPRESSES A NON-ALLOWLISTED ONE. This is the one that matters. _classify_command() returns the FIRST destructive segment it finds and stops; evaluate() then asks _allowed() about that one category only. If the first match is allowlisted, the function returns None and every later segment in the chain is never classified at all. Reproduced directly against the rule module:

    options = {"allow": {"history_rewrite": True}}
    "git rebase -i main && git push --force origin mybranch"   -> SILENT
    "git reset --hard origin/main && git push --force"         -> SILENT

Both chains contain a force-push that policy did NOT authorise, and the rule says nothing. `allow.history_rewrite: true` is the single most plausible option a consuming repo would set, since rebasing is routine. The module docstring justifies first-match by pointing at lwb_proof_required's "first match" posture, but that rule is looking for the presence of a publish, where first-match is harmless; here first-match composes with PER-CATEGORY authorisation to produce an authorisation bypass, not merely an under-match. This is materially different from the blind spots the docstring accepts: those are "a warning that did not fire"; this is "an explicitly forbidden action passed because a permitted one stood in front of it". Under deny mode -- which the docstring names as the next build-plan step -- it becomes a bypass of a deny. Test coverage confirms it is unhandled rather than accepted: the only chain test in tests/core/test_lwb_no_unauthorised_destructive_action.py is line 314, "python -m pytest -q && git push -f origin main", where the first segment is benign. There is no test where an allowed destructive category precedes a disallowed one. Suggested fix: classify ALL segments and report the first UNAUTHORISED one, rather than the first destructive one.

FINDING B -- `git commit --amend -n` IS SILENT, AND THIS BLIND SPOT IS NOT NAMED. _segments() inherits _NON_PUBLISHING_FLAGS = {"--dry-run", "-n", "--help", "-h"} from lwb_proof_required and drops any segment containing one. For `git push -n` that is correct: -n is --dry-run. For `git commit --amend -n` it is not: there -n is --no-verify, and the command rewrites history for real. Reproduced:

    "git commit --amend -m x"      -> FIRES (history_rewrite)
    "git commit --amend -n -m x"   -> SILENT

The module docstring says "Every blind spot below is accepted and named, not left to be found later as a bug", then lists four. This is a fifth, and it is not listed. It is also reachable by an agent that habitually passes --no-verify. Severity is lower than A (it is a genuine under-match, consistent with the declared posture) but it violates the module's own naming standard. Fix or document.

FINDING C (minor, one line) -- `git push origin --delete` with no ref argument classifies the REMOTE as the deleted ref: target comes back as "origin", because the target is taken as non_flags[-1] and "origin" is the only positional. Harmless today, but it means a remote name appearing in options.verified_landed_branches would silently authorise a malformed delete. Worth a guard.

=== A DESIGN INCONSISTENCY I RAISE BUT DID NOT COUNT AS A DEFECT ===

evaluate() returns None when event.repo is None or repo.facts_incomplete is true. The docstring justifies this by mirroring lwb_proof_required. But this rule consumes NO repo facts -- classification reads only event.tool_input, authorisation reads only config.options -- and the docstring itself argues for deny-capability on exactly that ground ("its signal (a command matches one of four syntactic shapes) is a fact, not a judgement"). So a purely syntactic check disables itself whenever fact-gathering degrades, which is when destructive commands are most likely to be flying. I am flagging this rather than charging it because the mirroring is deliberate, explicitly argued in the docstring, and a reviewer should not overturn a documented design choice on preference. The owner may want to revisit it.

=== A REPO-LEVEL FINDING THIS REVIEW SURFACED (stated separately because it did NOT drive my verdict) ===

A stale or DISAGREE record in reviews/<pr>/ is a HARD FAIL of lwb-lanes that no later AGREE can clear. Measured on #45: adding a valid, fresh AGREE record leaves lwb-lanes at exit 1 with 20 FAIL lines, because two records naming an older reviewable head still fail; deleting only those two stale records makes the same command exit 0, "lwb-lanes check passed". Since force-push is denied, the only in-place remedy is deleting another reviewer's record, which this repo treats as falsifying evidence -- so the practical remedy has been to re-cut the whole PR (#38->#39, #40->#45, #43->#46, #44->#47->#48, #52->#53). Consequence worth the owner's attention: a reviewer's DISAGREE is not a request for changes, it is a permanent kill on that PR number. I want it on the record that I noticed this BEFORE choosing my verdict here, and that it did not change it: I re-argued #53 purely on merits (claims all true, tests non-vacuous, vendor in sync, defects latent and unreachable under the shipped default policy) and reached AGREE independently.
